title: Ceph Block Device
content:
The most popular use of IBM Storage Ceph, the Ceph
Block Device interface, also referred to as RADOS Block Device, or RBD, creates virtual volumes,
images, and compute instances and stores them as a series of objects within pools. Ceph assigns
these objects to placement groups and distributes or places them pseudo-randomly in OSDs throughout
the cluster.

Depending upon the application consuming the Ceph Block Device interface, usually OpenStack
Platform, users may create, modify, and delete volumes and images. Ceph handles the create,
retrieve, update, and delete operations of each individual object.

Deleting volumes and images destroys the corresponding objects in an unrecoverable manner.
However, residual data artifacts may continue to reside on storage media until overwritten. Data may
also remain in backup archives.
section_path: Ceph Block Device

title: NVMe over Fabrics
content:
Ceph Block Device now offers NVMe-oF gateway support. Non-Volatile Memory express (NVMe) and NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) protocols are designed specifically to enable the full capabilities of parallelism and performance with all-flash storage systems.

NVMe-oF enables the performance of direct attached all-flash storage along with the flexibility and total cost of ownership (TCO) savings of shared storage. Implementing NVMe-oF support in enterprise storage arrays allows the combination of the NVMe protocol performance with the rich feature set of modern storage arrays. Using NVMe protocol enables modern storage arrays to meet growing customer demands.

NVMe-oF uses the TCP protocol as a ubiquitous transport that does not require special network configuration, by using existing Ethernet connectivity. Ethernet speeds currently support up to 400 Gib per second and the use of Ethernet technology is significant in data centers.

For more information about Ceph Block Device NVMe-oF gateway support, see Ceph NVMe-oF gateway.
section_path: NVMe over Fabrics

title: Ceph Block Devices
content:
Learn to manage, create, configure, and use IBM Storage Ceph Block Devices.

A block is a set length of bytes in a sequence, for example, a 512-byte block of data. Combining many blocks together into a single file can be used as a storage device that you can read from and write to. Block-based storage interfaces are the most common way to store data with rotating media such as:
 
- Hard drives
- CD/DVD discs
- Floppy disks
- Traditional 9-track tapes

Ceph Block Devices are thin-provisioned, resizable and store data striped over multiple Object Storage Devices (OSD) in a Ceph storage cluster. Ceph Block Devices are also known as Reliable Autonomic Distributed Object Store (RADOS) Block Devices (RBDs). Ceph Block Devices leverage RADOS capabilities such as:

- Snapshots
- Replication
- Data consistency

Ceph Block Devices interact with OSDs by using the `librbd` library.

Ceph Block Devices deliver high performance with infinite scalability to Kernel Virtual Machines (KVMs), such as Quick Emulator (QEMU), and cloud-based computing systems, like OpenStack, that rely on the `libvirt` and QEMU utilities to integrate with Ceph Block Devices. You can use the same storage cluster to operate the Ceph Object Gateway and Ceph Block Devices simultaneously.
 
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Using Ceph Block Devices requires access to a running Ceph storage cluster. For more information about installing an IBM Storage Ceph cluster, see Initial installation.
section_path: Ceph Block Devices

title: Creating block device pools
content: Learn how to create a block device pool.
section_path: Creating block device pools

title: Before you begin
content:
Before using the block device client, ensure a pool for `rbd` exists, is enabled and initialized.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You **MUST** create a pool first before you can specify it as a source.

 Before beginning this procedure, ensure that you have the following:

- Root-level access to the client node.

title: About this task
content: For more information, see Pools.
section_path: Creating block device pools > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Create a Ceph Block Device (`rbd`) pool.

```bash
ceph osd pool create POOL_NAME PG_NUM
 
ceph osd pool application enable POOL_NAME rbd
rbd pool init -p POOL_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# ceph osd pool create pool1
[root@rbd-client ~]# ceph osd pool application enable pool1 rbd
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd pool init -p pool1
```

title: rbdmap service
content:
The `systemd` unit file, `rbdmap.service`, is included with
the `ceph-common` package. The `rbdmap.service` unit runs the
`rbdmap` shell script. This script automates the mapping and unmapping of RADOS Block
Devices (RBD) for one or more RBD images.

The `rbdmap` script can be ran manually at any time, but the typical use case is
to automatically mount RBD images at boot time, and unmount at shutdown. The script takes a single
argument, which can be either `map`, for mounting or `unmap`, for
unmounting RBD images. The script parses a configuration file, the default is
`/etc/ceph/rbdmap`, but can be overridden using an environment variable called
`RBDMAPFILE`. Each line of the configuration file corresponds to an RBD image.

The format of the configuration file format is as follows:

`IMAGE_SPEC RBD_OPTS`

Where` IMAGE_SPEC` specifies the `POOL_NAME / IMAGE_NAME`, or just
the `IMAGE_NAME`, in which case the `POOL_NAME` defaults to
`rbd`. The R`BD_OPTS` is an optional list of options to be passed to
the underlying `rbd map` command. These parameters and their values should be
specified as a comma-separated string:

`OPT1=VAL1,OPT2=VAL2,...,OPT_N=VAL_N`

This will cause the script to issue an `rbd map` command like the following:

Syntax

```bash
rbd map POOL_NAME/IMAGE_NAME --OPT1 VAL1 --OPT2 VAL2
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For options and values which contain commas or equality signs, a simple apostrophe can be used
to prevent replacing them.

When successful, the `rbd map` operation maps the image to a
`/dev/rbdX` device, at which point a `udev` rule is triggered to
create a friendly device name symlink, for example, `/dev/rbd/POOL_NAME/IMAGE_NAME`,
pointing to the real mapped device. For mounting or unmounting to succeed, the friendly device name
must have a corresponding entry in `/etc/fstab` file. When writing
`/etc/fstab` entries for RBD images, it is a good idea to specify the
`noauto` or `nofail` mount option. This prevents the init system from
trying to mount the device too early, before the device exists.
section_path: rbdmap service

title: Reference
content: - See the `rbd` manpage for a full list of possible options.
section_path: rbdmap service > Reference

title: Configuring rbdmap service
content:
Automatically map and mount, or unmap and unmount, RADOS Block Devices (RBD) at boot
time, or at shutdown respectively.
section_path: Configuring rbdmap service

title: Prerequisites
content:
- Root-level access to the node doing the mounting.
- Installation of the `ceph-common` package.
section_path: Configuring rbdmap service > Prerequisites

title: Procedure
content:
1. Open for editing the `/etc/ceph/rbdmap` configuration file.
2. Add the RBD image or images to the configuration file:

Example

```bash
foo/bar1 id=admin,keyring=/etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring
foo/bar2 id=admin,keyring=/etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring,options='lock_on_read,queue_depth=1024'
```
3. Save changes to the configuration file.
4. Enable the RBD mapping service:

Example

```bash
[root@client ~]# systemctl enable rbdmap.service
```

content: For more information about the RBD system service, see rbdmap service.

title: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces
content: Ceph Block Device namespaces provide logical isolation for block device images within a pool. A namespace enables isolation of images for different applications, tenants, or workloads without requiring separate pools.
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Ensure that the target pool exists.
- Ensure that you have appropriate permissions to manage Ceph Block Device resources.
- Ensure that the Ceph cluster is accessible from the command-line interface.
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Each namespace exists within a pool and is referenced as part of the image specification. You can create, list, remove, and use namespaces to organize Ceph Block Device images within a pool.

Using namespaces provides the following benefits:

- Logical separation of images within a pool.
- Improved organization of resources.
- Multi-tenant isolation within the same pool.
- Simplified management of large numbers of images.

An image-spec can be identified by using the following syntax:

```bash
[POOL_NAME/[NAMESPACE/]]IMAGE
```

Where,

- The default for POOL_NAME is `rbd`
- The default for NAMESPACE is "". When no namespace is specified, the image resides in the default namespace.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 POOL_NAME is required if an image name contains a slash character (/).
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > About this task

title: Creating a namespace
content: Create a new namespace within an existing pool to logically isolate block device images for specific applications or tenants.
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > Creating a namespace

title: Procedure
content:
Create a namespace within a pool.

```bash
rbd namespace create POOL_NAME/NAMESPACE
```

For example,

```
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd namespace create mypool/dev
```
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify that the namespace is created by listing namespaces in a pool. Check that the namespace is listed in the output.
 
```bash
rbd namespace list POOL_NAME
```
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > What to do next

title: Removing a namespace
content: Delete a namespace from a pool when it is no longer needed. The namespace must be empty before removal.
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > Removing a namespace

title: Procedure
content:
1. Ensure that the namespace is empty.

```bash
rbd ls -p POOL_NAME --namespace NAMESPACE
```

The output should be empty. If any images are listed, the namespace is not empty.

- If the output is empty, continue to step 3.
- If the output contains remaining images, continue to step 2.
2. If needed, remove any images within the namespace.

1. Remove the images.

```bash
rbd rm -p POOL_NAME --namespace NAMESPACE IMAGE_NAME
```
2. Verify that the namespace is empty.

Repeat step 1 and 2a until no images are listed.
3. Remove the namespace.

```bash
rbd namespace remove POOL_NAME/NAMESPACE
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd namespace remove mypool/dev
```
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify that the namespace is removed.

```bash
rbd namespace list POOL_NAME
```

The namespace will no longer be listed in the output.
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > What to do next

title: Using namespaces in Ceph Block Device operations
content: Use a namespace to scope Ceph Block Device commands to a specific group of images within a pool, either by including the namespace in the image path or by using the --namespace option.
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > Using namespaces in Ceph Block Device operations

title: About this task
content:
Both methods are functionally equivalent. When using these commands:

- Always specify both the pool and the namespace to avoid ambiguity.
- Use the --namespace option when scripting or when you want to separate the namespace from the image path.
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Choose one of the following methods to create an image in a namespace.

- Specify the namespace in the image path.

```bash
rbd create POOL_NAME/NAMESPACE/IMAGE --size SIZE
```

For example,

```
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd create mypool/dev/myimage --size 10240
```

This command creates the image `myimage` in the `dev` namespace within the `mypool` pool.
- Use the --namespace option.

```bash
rbd --namespace NAMESPACE -p POOL_NAME create IMAGE --size SIZE
```

For example,

```
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd --namespace dev -p mypool create myimage --size 10240
```

This command creates the image `myimage` in the `dev` namespace within the `mypool` pool.
section_path: Managing Ceph Block Device namespaces > Procedure

title: Ceph Block Device layering
content:
Ceph supports the ability to create many copy-on-write (COW) or copy-on-read (COR) clones
of a block device snapshot. Snapshot layering enables Ceph Block Device clients to create images
very quickly.

For example, you might create a block device image with a Linux VM written to it. Then, snapshot
the image, protect the snapshot, and create as many clones as you like. A snapshot is read-only, so
cloning a snapshot simplifies semantics—making it possible to create clones rapidly.

Figure 1. Ceph Block Device layering

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The terms `parent` and `child` mean a Ceph Block Device
snapshot, parent, and the corresponding image cloned from the snapshot, child. These terms are
important for the command line usage below.

Each cloned image, the child, stores a reference to its parent image, which enables the cloned
image to open the parent snapshot and read it. This reference is removed when the clone is
`flattened` that is, when information from the snapshot is completely copied to the
clone.

A clone of a snapshot behaves exactly like any other Ceph Block Device image. You can read to,
write from, clone, and resize the cloned images. There are no special restrictions with cloned
images. However, the clone of a snapshot refers to the snapshot, so you **MUST** protect the
snapshot before you clone it.

A clone of a snapshot can be a copy-on-write (COW) or copy-on-read (COR) clone. Copy-on-write
(COW) is always enabled for clones while copy-on-read (COR) has to be enabled explicitly.
Copy-on-write (COW) copies data from the parent to the clone when it writes to an unallocated object
within the clone. Copy-on-read (COR) copies data from the parent to the clone when it reads from an
unallocated object within the clone. Reading data from a clone will only read data from the parent
if the object does not yet exist in the clone. Rados block device breaks up large images into
multiple objects. The default is set to 4 MB and all copy-on-write (COW) and copy-on-read (COR)
operations occur on a full object, that is writing 1 byte to a clone will result in a 4 MB object
being read from the parent and written to the clone if the destination object does not already exist
in the clone from a previous COW/COR operation.

Whether or not copy-on-read (COR) is enabled, any reads that cannot be satisfied by reading an
underlying object from the clone will be rerouted to the parent. Since there is practically no limit
to the number of parents, meaning that you can clone a clone, this reroute continues until an object
is found or you hit the base parent image. If copy-on-read (COR) is enabled, any reads that fail to
be satisfied directly from the clone result in a full object read from the parent and writing that
data to the clone so that future reads of the same extent can be satisfied from the clone itself
without the need of reading from the parent.

This is essentially an on-demand, object-by-object flatten operation. This is specially useful
when the clone is in a high-latency connection away from it’s parent, that is the parent in a
different pool, in another geographical location. Copy-on-read (COR) reduces the amortized latency
of reads. The first few reads will have high latency because it will result in extra data being read
from the parent, for example, you read 1 byte from the clone but now 4 MB has to be read from the
parent and written to the clone, but all future reads will be served from the clone itself.

To create copy-on-read (COR) clones from snapshot you have to explicitly enable this feature by
adding `rbd_clone_copy_on_read = true` under `[global]` or
`[client]` section in the `ceph.conf` file.

title: Cloning block device snapshot
content:
Cloning block device snapshots provides an efficient way to create writable copies of
existing block device snapshots without duplicating data. You can either clone a single block device
snapshot or a group block device snapshot based on your requirement.
section_path: Cloning block device snapshot

title: Cloning a single block device snapshot
content:
Clone a block device snapshot to create a read or write child image of the snapshot
within the same pool or in another pool. One use case would be to maintain read-only images and
snapshots as templates in one pool, and writable clones in another pool.
section_path: Cloning a single block device snapshot

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to the node.
section_path: Cloning a single block device snapshot > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Clone v2 does not require protection of snapshots.
section_path: Cloning a single block device snapshot > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Clone a snapshot. To clone a snapshot, specify the parent pool, snapshot, child pool, and image
name.
```bash
rbd clone --pool POOL_NAME --image PARENT_IMAGE --snap SNAP_NAME --dest-pool POOL_NAME --dest CHILD_IMAGE_NAME
rbd clone POOL_NAME/PARENT_IMAGE@SNAP_NAME POOL_NAME/CHILD_IMAGE_NAME
```
For
example,
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd clone --pool pool1 --image image1 --snap snap1 --dest-pool pool1 --dest childimage1
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd clone pool1/image1@snap1 pool1/childimage1
```

content:

The following example has a group snapshot, indicated with `SNAPID` listed as

title: Configuring Ceph Block Device mirroring
content: Configure one-way and two-way replication of a Ceph Block Device (`rbd`) pool to enable data synchronization between the primary storage cluster and a secondary cluster by using the command-line interface.
section_path: Configuring Ceph Block Device mirroring

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A minimum of two running IBM Storage Ceph clusters.
- Root-level access to a Ceph client node for each storage cluster.
- A CephX user with administrator-level capabilities.
section_path: Configuring Ceph Block Device mirroring > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- When using one-way replication, you can mirror to multiple secondary storage clusters.
- When using two-way replication you can only mirror between two storage clusters.

Examples in this section distinguish between two storage clusters by referring to the primary storage cluster with the primary images as `site-a`, and the secondary storage cluster you are replicating the images to, as `site-b`. The pool name that is used in these examples is called `data`.
section_path: Configuring Ceph Block Device mirroring > About this task

title: Journal-based mirroring
content: Configure asynchronous replication for a block image using Ceph Block Device journaling to ensure near real-time, crash-consistent synchronization between clusters.
section_path: Configuring Ceph Block Device mirroring > Journal-based mirroring

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to the `cephadm` shell on both the sites.
For example,
 
```
[root@site-a ~]# cephadm shell
[root@site-b ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. On `site-b`, schedule the deployment of mirror daemon on the secondary cluster.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- For two-way replication, repeat this step on site-a.
- For one-way replication, continue to step 3.

```bash
ceph orch apply rbd-mirror --placement=NODENAME
```

Where NODENAME is the host where you want to configure mirroring in the secondary cluster.

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@site-b /]# ceph orch apply rbd-mirror --placement=host04
```
3. Enable journaling features on an image on `site-a`.

1. Use the --image-feature option for new images.

```bash
rbd create IMAGE_NAME --size MEGABYTES --pool POOL_NAME --image-feature FEATURE FEATURE
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If `exclusive-lock` is already enabled, use `journaling` as the only argument, else it returns the following error:one or more requested features are already enabled (22) Invalid argument

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@site-a /]# rbd create image1 --size 1024 --pool data --image-feature exclusive-lock,journaling
```
2. Use the rbd feature enable command for existing images.
Syntax,
 
```bash
rbd feature enable POOL_NAME/IMAGE_NAME FEATURE, FEATURE
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@site-a /]# rbd feature enable data/image1 exclusive-lock, journaling
```
3. Enable journaling on all new images by default.
Set the configuration parameter by using the ceph config set command. 
For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@site-a /]# ceph config set global rbd_default_features 125
[ceph: root@site-a /]# ceph config show mon.host01 rbd_default_features
```
4. Choose the mirroring mode on both the storage clusters.
 The mode can be either pool or image.
 
```bash
rbd mirror pool enable POOL_NAME MODE
```

 Use one of the following options, enabling either with pool or image, based on your requirements.

- The following example enables mirroring of the whole pool named `data`.
 
```
[ceph: root@site-a /]# rbd mirror pool enable data pool
[ceph: root@site-b /]# rbd mirror pool enable data pool
```
- The following example enables image mode mirroring on the pool named `data`.
 
```
[ceph: root@site-a /]# rbd mirror pool enable data image
[ceph: root@site-b /]# rbd mirror pool enable data image
```
5. Verify that mirroring is successfully enabled at both the sites. 

```bash
rbd mirror pool info POOL_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@site-a /]# rbd mirror pool info data
Mode: pool
Site Name: c13d8065-b33d-4cb5-b35f-127a02768e7f

Peer Sites: none

[ceph: root@site-b /]# rbd mirror pool info data
Mode: pool
Site Name: a4c667e2-b635-47ad-b462-6faeeee78df7

Peer Sites: none
```
6. On the Ceph client node, bootstrap the storage cluster peers.

1. Create Ceph user accounts, and register the storage cluster peer to the pool.

```bash
rbd mirror pool peer bootstrap create --site-name PRIMARY_LOCAL_SITE_NAME POOL_NAME > PATH_TO_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN
```

The following example bootstrap command creates the `client.rbd-mirror.site-a` and the `client.rbd-mirror-peer` Ceph users.
 
```
[ceph: root@rbd-client-site-a /]# rbd mirror pool peer bootstrap create --site-name site-a data > /root/bootstrap_token_site-a
```
2. Copy the bootstrap token file to the `site-b` storage cluster.
3. Import the bootstrap token on the `site-b` storage cluster.

```bash
bd mirror pool peer bootstrap import --site-name SECONDARY_LOCAL_SITE_NAME --direction rx-only POOL_NAME PATH_TO_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@rbd-client-site-b /]# rbd mirror pool peer bootstrap import --site-name site-b --direction rx-only data /root/bootstrap_token_site-a
```

title: Snapshot-based mirroring
content: Set up periodic replication for a block image by creating and syncing snapshots to provide point-in-time consistency across clusters.

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to the `cephadm` shell on both the sites.
For example,
 
```
[root@site-a ~]# cephadm shell
[root@site-b ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. On `site-b`, schedule the deployment of mirror daemon on the secondary cluster.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- For two-way replication, repeat this step on site-a.
- For one-way replication, continue to step 3.

```bash
ceph orch apply rbd-mirror --placement=NODENAME
```

Where NODENAME is the host where you want to configure mirroring in the secondary cluster.

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@site-b /]# ceph orch apply rbd-mirror --placement=host04
```
3. Enable image mode mirroring on the pool.

```bash
rbd mirror pool enable POOL_NAME MODE
```

The following example enables image mode mirroring on the pool named `data`.
 
```
[ceph: root@site-a /]# rbd mirror pool enable data image
[ceph: root@site-b /]# rbd mirror pool enable data image
```
4. Verify that mirroring is successfully enabled at both the sites. 

```bash
rbd mirror pool info POOL_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@site-a /]# rbd mirror pool data
Mode: pool
Site Name: c13d8065-b33d-4cb5-b35f-127a02768e7f
Mirror UUID: be874515-c563-4bb0-a24a-962a2784c665
Remote Namesapace:

Peer Sites: none

[ceph: root@site-b /]# rbd mirror pool info data
Mode: pool
Site Name: a4c667e2-b635-47ad-b462-6faeeee78df7
Mirror UUID: be874515-c563-4bb0-a24a-962a2784c665

Peer Sites: none
```
5. On the Ceph client node, bootstrap the storage cluster peers.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For two-way mirroring, repeat these substeps in opposite order. First creating a bootstrap on `site-b` and then importing on `site-a`.

1. Create Ceph user accounts, and register the storage cluster peer to the pool.

```bash
rbd mirror pool peer bootstrap create --site-name PRIMARY_LOCAL_SITE_NAME POOL_NAME > PATH_TO_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN
```

The following example bootstrap command creates the `client.rbd-mirror.site-a` and the `client.rbd-mirror-peer` Ceph users.
 
```
[ceph: root@rbd-client-site-a /]# rbd mirror pool peer bootstrap create --site-name site-a data > /root/bootstrap_token_site-a
```
2. Copy the bootstrap token file to the `site-b` storage cluster.
3. Import the bootstrap token on the `site-b` storage cluster.

```bash
rbd mirror pool peer bootstrap import --site-name SECONDARY_LOCAL_SITE_NAME --direction rx-only POOL_NAME PATH_TO_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@rbd-client-site-b /]# rbd mirror pool peer bootstrap import --site-name site-b --direction rx-only data /root/bootstrap_token_site-a
```
6. On the Primary site, create a new Ceph Block Device image in a specific pool.

```bash
rbd create POOL_NAME/IMAGE_NAME --size SIZE
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@rbd-client-site-a /]# rbd create data/image1 --size 1024
```
7. Enable snapshot image mirroring.

```bash
rbd mirror image enable POOL_NAME/IMAGE_NAME snapshot
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@rbd-client-site-a /]# rbd mirror image enable data/image1 snapshot
```
8. Create a snapshot mirror schedule.

```bash
rbd --cluster CLUSTER_NAME mirror snapshot schedule add --pool POOL_NAME --image IMAGE_NAME INTERVAL
```

 For more information, see Scheduling mirror snapshots.
For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@rbd-client-site-a /]# rbd --cluster site-a mirror snapshot schedule add --pool data --image image1 6h
```

title: Administering Ceph Block Device mirroring
content:
As a storage administrator, you can perform a range of tasks to manage and maintain the Ceph Block Device (RBD) mirroring environment.

These tasks include:

- Viewing information about storage cluster peers.
- Add or remove a storage cluster peer.
- Getting mirroring status for a pool, image and group.
- Enabling mirroring on a pool, image and group.
- Disabling mirroring on a pool, image and group.
- Delaying block device replication.
- Promoting and demoting an image and group.

These tasks help ensure smooth replication operations and support failover and recovery scenarios in multi-site deployments.

title: Delaying block device replication
content: Learn to delay block device replication by using the command-line.
section_path: Delaying block device replication

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to the node.
section_path: Delaying block device replication > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Whether using one-way or two-way replication, you can configure delayed replication for RADOS
Block Device (RBD) mirrored images. Delayed replication provides a buffer period, allowing you to
revert unintended changes on the primary image before they are propagated to the secondary
image.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Delaying block device replication is only applicable with journal-based mirroring.

To implement delayed replication, the `rbd-mirror` daemon within the destination
storage cluster should set the `rbd_mirroring_replay_delay =
_MINIMUM_DELAY_IN_SECONDS_` configuration option. This setting can either be applied
globally within the ceph.conf file utilized by the `rbd-mirror`
daemons, or on an individual image basis.
section_path: Delaying block device replication > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Utilize delayed replication for a specific image, on the primary image by running the
following rbd
command.Syntax,
```bash
rbd image-meta set POOL_NAME/IMAGE_NAME conf_rbd_mirroring_replay_delay MINIMUM_DELAY_IN_SECONDS
```
The
following example sets a 10 minute minimum replication delay on image `vm-1` in the
`vms`
pool.
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd image-meta set vms/vm-1 conf_rbd_mirroring_replay_delay 600
```
section_path: Delaying block device replication > Procedure

title: Configure graceful shutdown for rbd-mirror
content:
Configure `rbd-mirror` for immediate shutdown to interrupt Ceph Block Device replication tasks and enable fast failover during maintenance or orchestration updates.

When you manage `rbd-mirror` services, you might need to control how quickly the daemon shuts down during orchestration updates or failover events. Use the termination_grace_period_seconds option in the service specification to set the time, in seconds, that a daemon can terminate gracefully before it is forcefully stopped.

A long grace period can delay `rbd-mirror` shutdown and affect automated failover processes.

To ensure fast failover, set termination_grace_period_seconds to 0 in the rbd-mirror service specification.

```bash
service_type: rbd-mirror
placement:
 count: 1
spec:
 termination_grace_period_seconds: 0
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 External tools, such as IBM Storage Ceph Storage Replication Adapter, rely on quick termination to avoid hung states. When you use SRA, configure termination_grace_period_seconds to 0 so the daemon exits immediately when required.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- Other services, such as OSDs, can retain defaults as high as 30 seconds for a clean shutdown.
- This setting is propagated into systemd unit files and affects daemon termination during orchestration updates or failover events.
section_path: Configure graceful shutdown for rbd-mirror

title: rbd kernel module
content:
Access Ceph Block Devices through the `rbd` kernel module. Through the module, you can map and unmap a Block Device and display the mappings. A list of images can also be retrieved through the `rbd` kernel module.

 Kernel clients on Linux distributions other than Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) are permitted but not supported. If issues are found in the storage cluster when using these kernel clients, IBM addresses them, but if the root cause is found to be on the kernel client side, the issue will have to be addressed by the software vendor.

title: Map and mount a Ceph Block Device on Linux using the command-line
content: Map and mount a Ceph Block Device to enable writing files to it by using the command-line interface.
section_path: Map and mount a Ceph Block Device on Linux using the command-line

title: Before you begin
content:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- A Ceph Block Device for a Linux kernel module client that uses the dashboard is created.
- A Red Hat Enterprise Linux client.
section_path: Map and mount a Ceph Block Device on Linux using the command-line > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. On the Red Hat Enterprise Linux client node, enable the IBM Storage Ceph tools repository.

```bash
subscription-manager repos --enable=ibmceph-9-tools-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms
```

For example,
 
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# subscription-manager repos --enable=ibmceph-9-tools-for-rhel-9-x86_64-rpms
```
2. Install the `ceph-common` RPM package.

```bash
dnf install ceph-common
```
3. Copy the Ceph configuration file from a Monitor node to the Client node.

```bash
scp root@MONITOR_NODE:/etc/ceph/ceph.conf /etc/ceph/ceph.conf
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# scp root@cluster1-node2:/etc/ceph/ceph.conf /etc/ceph/ceph.conf
root@192.168.0.32's password:
ceph.conf 100% 497 724.9KB/s 00:00
```
4. Copy the key file from a Monitor node to the Client node.

```bash
scp root@MONITOR_NODE:/etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring /etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# scp root@cluster1-node2:/etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring /etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring
root@192.168.0.32's password:
ceph.client.admin.keyring 100% 151 265.0KB/s 00:00
```
5. Map the image.

```bash
rbd map --pool POOL_NAME IMAGE_NAME --id admin
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# rbd map --pool block-device-pool image1 --id admin
/dev/rbd0
```
6. Create a partition table on the block device.

```bash
parted /dev/MAPPED_BLOCK_DEVICE mklabel msdos
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# parted /dev/rbd0 mklabel msdos
Information: You may need to update /etc/fstab.
```
7. Create a partition for an XFS file system.

```bash
parted /dev/MAPPED_BLOCK_DEVICE mkpart primary xfs 0% 100%
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# parted /dev/rbd0 mkpart primary xfs 0% 100%
Information: You may need to update /etc/fstab.
```
8. Format the partition.

```bash
mkfs.xfs /dev/MAPPED_BLOCK_DEVICE_WITH_PARTITION_NUMBER
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# mkfs.xfs /dev/rbd0p1
meta-data=/dev/rbd0p1 isize=512 agcount=16, agsize=163824 blks
 = sectsz=512 attr=2, projid32bit=1
 = crc=1 finobt=1, sparse=1, rmapbt=0
 = reflink=1
data = bsize=4096 blocks=2621184, imaxpct=25
 = sunit=16 swidth=16 blks
naming =version 2 bsize=4096 ascii-ci=0, ftype=1
log =internal log bsize=4096 blocks=2560, version=2
 = sectsz=512 sunit=16 blks, lazy-count=1
realtime =none extsz=4096 blocks=0, rtextents=0
```
9. Create a directory to mount the new file system on.

```bash
mkdir PATH_TO_DIRECTORY
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# mkdir /mnt/ceph
```
10. Mount the file system.

```bash
mount /dev/MAPPED_BLOCK_DEVICE_WITH_PARTITION_NUMBER PATH_TO_DIRECTORY
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# mount /dev/rbd0p1 /mnt/ceph/
```
11. Verify that the file system is mounted and showing the correct size.

```bash
df -h PATH_TO_DIRECTORY
```

For example,
 
```
[root@rbd-client ~]# df -h /mnt/ceph/
Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/rbd0p1 10G 105M 9.9G 2% /mnt/ceph
```

title: Ceph Block Device python module
content:
The `rbd` python module provides file-like access to Ceph Block Device
images. In order to use this built-in tool, import the `rbd` and
`rados` python modules.
section_path: Ceph Block Device python module

title: Prerequisites
content:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to the node.
section_path: Ceph Block Device python module > Prerequisites

title: Procedure
content:
1. Connect to RADOS and open an IO context:

```bash
cluster = rados.Rados(conffile='my_ceph.conf')
cluster.connect()
ioctx = cluster.open_ioctx('mypool')
```
2. Instantiate an `:class:rbd.RBD` object, which you use to create the image:

```bash
rbd_inst = rbd.RBD()
size = 4 * 1024**3 # 4 GiB
rbd_inst.create(ioctx, 'myimage', size)
```
3. To perform I/O on the image, instantiate an `:class:rbd.Image` object:

```bash
image = rbd.Image(ioctx, 'myimage')
data = 'foo' * 200
image.write(data, 0)
```

This writes *foo* to the first 600 bytes of the image. Note that data cannot be
`:type:unicode` - `librbd` does not know how to deal with characters
wider than a `:c:type:char`.
4. Close the image, the IO context and the connection to RADOS:

```bash
image.close()
ioctx.close()
cluster.shutdown()
```

To be safe, each of these calls must to be in a separate `:finally` block:

```bash
import rados
import rbd

cluster = rados.Rados(conffile='my_ceph_conf')
try:
 ioctx = cluster.open_ioctx('my_pool')
 try:
 rbd_inst = rbd.RBD()
 size = 4 * 1024**3 # 4 GiB
 rbd_inst.create(ioctx, 'myimage', size)
 image = rbd.Image(ioctx, 'myimage')
 try:
 data = 'foo' * 200
 image.write(data, 0)
 finally:
 image.close()
 finally:
 ioctx.close()
finally:
 cluster.shutdown()
```

This can be cumbersome, so the **Rados**, **Ioctx**, and **Image** classes can be used
as context managers that close or shut down automatically. Using them as context managers, the above
example becomes:

```bash
with rados.Rados(conffile='my_ceph.conf') as cluster:
 with cluster.open_ioctx('mypool') as ioctx:
 rbd_inst = rbd.RBD()
 size = 4 * 1024**3 # 4 GiB
 rbd_inst.create(ioctx, 'myimage', size)
 with rbd.Image(ioctx, 'myimage') as image:
 data = 'foo' * 200
 image.write(data, 0)
```

title: Ceph Block Devices and OpenStack
content:
IBM Storage Ceph integration with Red Hat OpenStack provides scalable and resilient block storage for cloud workloads, supporting virtual machine images, volumes, and guest disks.

IBM Storage Ceph integrates with OpenStack distributed block storage backend that scales horizontally and delivers high availability for cloud workloads. In an integrated environment, Ceph Block Devices are consumed by multiple OpenStack services, to store and manage images, volumes, persistent and virtual machine disks efficiently.

This section describes the supported integration models between Ceph and OpenStack, the OpenStack services that can use Ceph block storage, and key considerations to review before configuring the environment.

For detailed deployment guidance and service‑specific configuration options, see the Red Hat OpenStack Platform documentation for your specific OpenStack release.
section_path: Ceph Block Devices and OpenStack

title: Ceph and OpenStack integration models
content:
OpenStack can use Ceph Block Devices in the following deployment models:

OpenStack‑managed Ceph cluster
In this model, OpenStack creates and manages the Ceph storage cluster as part of the deployment. OpenStack installs and configures Ceph components, including monitors and object storage daemons (OSDs). This approach simplifies deployment by allowing OpenStack to automate Ceph installation and configuration. 
Existing Ceph cluster integration
OpenStack connects to a preconfigured Ceph storage cluster and uses existing Ceph monitors. Ceph block devices are configured as a storage backend for OpenStack services. This model is typically used when a Ceph cluster already exists or when storage and cloud infrastructure are managed separately. 

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The procedures described in this guide assume that you are manually configuring OpenStack to use an existing Ceph cluster rather than using automated deployment tools such as an OpenStack director.
section_path: Ceph Block Devices and OpenStack > Ceph and OpenStack integration models

title: OpenStack services that use Ceph Block Devices
content:
Ceph Block Devices can be used as storage backends for several OpenStack services:

Image storage (Glance)
OpenStack Glance manages virtual machine images, which are treated as immutable objects. When Glance is configured to use Ceph, images are stored in a Ceph Block Device pool and can be efficiently cloned using copy-on-write mechanisms. 
Volume storage (Cinder and Cinder Backup)
OpenStack Cinder provides persistent block storage volumes that can be attached to running virtual machines, used for boot-from-volume instances, or backed up using Cinder Backup. Ceph can be used as a backend for both Cinder volumes and Cinder Backup storage. 
Guest virtual machine disks (Nova)
Ceph block devices can store guest virtual machine disks directly. Instead of maintaining disk files on the hypervisor file system, Nova accesses disks from Ceph, improving scalability and enabling features such as live migration.
section_path: Ceph Block Devices and OpenStack > OpenStack services that use Ceph Block Devices

title: Image format and storage considerations
content:
Ceph does not support the QCOW2 image format for hosting virtual machine disks. To boot virtual machines using Ceph block storage, images configured in Glance must use the RAW format.

This requirement applies to both ephemeral disks and boot‑from‑volume instances.

OpenStack can use Ceph for any combination of image storage, volume storage, or guest disk storage. There is no requirement to use Ceph for all three services.

As a storage administrator, you must configure OpenStack services to use Ceph Block Devices after installing and preparing the Ceph cluster. This configuration enables OpenStack components to consume Ceph storage for images, volumes, backups, and virtual machine disks.

This section describes the tasks required to configure OpenStack components to integrate with Ceph block storage. Complete all tasks in this section only after Ceph is fully installed and configured for OpenStack.

- Ceph storage pools required for OpenStack service integration are created.
- Ceph client authentication is configured.
- A running OpenStack environment is available.

title: Ceph NVMe-oF gateway
content:
Storage administrators can install and configure an NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) gateway for an IBM Storage Ceph cluster. With Ceph NVMe-oF gateways, you can effectively run a fully integrated block storage infrastructure with all features and benefits of a conventional Storage Area Network (SAN).

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- The NVMe-oF gateway supports VMware vSphere APIs (VAAI), which includes support for vMotion, compare and write, unmap, and write zero.
- NVMe reserve is supported for host clustering.

Block-level access to a Ceph storage cluster used to be limited to QEMU and `librbd`. Block-level access to the Ceph storage cluster can now take advantage of the NVMe-oF standard to provide data storage.

Use the Ceph Dashboard to easily configure and manage the Ceph NVMe-oF gateway. For more information, see Managing the Ceph NVMe-oF gateway.

The NVMe-oF gateway integrates IBM Storage Ceph with the NVMe over TCP (NVMe/TCP) protocol to provide an NVMe/TCP target that exports Ceph Block Device (RBD) images. The NVMe/TCP protocol allows clients, which are known as initiators, to send NVMe-oF commands to storage devices, which are known as targets, over an Internet Protocol network. Initiators can be Linux clients, VMware clients, or both. For VMware clients, the NVMe/TCP volumes are shown as VMFS Datastore and for Linux clients, the NVMe/TCP volumes are shown as block devices.

Figure 1. Ceph NVMe-oF gateway

For more information about the NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) protocol, see NVMe over Fabrics.
section_path: Ceph NVMe-oF gateway

title: NVMe-oF in a stretch cluster
content:
An NVMe-oF stretch cluster extends an IBM Storage Ceph deployment across two sites to provide continuous NVMe-over-Fabrics block storage access during site-level failures and planned workload movement.

In a stretch cluster configuration, Ceph storage nodes and NVMe-oF gateways are distributed across two sites, commonly referred to as Site A and Site B. The sites are connected by a network with controlled latency, typically in the range of 2–10 milliseconds.

NVMe-oF initiators, such as VMware ESXi hosts, access Ceph Block Device (RBD) storage through NVMe-oF gateways deployed in both sites. The stretch cluster architecture is designed to support business continuity and disaster recovery (BCDR) use cases, including infrastructure failures, planned maintenance, and controlled migration of workloads between sites.

For more information about stretch cluster behavior, supported architectures, and failure scenarios, see NVMe-oF in a stretch cluster.

For general information about using IBM Storage Ceph stretch clusters, see Stretch clusters for Ceph storage.
section_path: Ceph NVMe-oF gateway > NVMe-oF in a stretch cluster

title: High Availability with NVMe-oF gateway group
content:
High Availability (HA) provides I/O and control path redundancies for the host initiators. High Availability is also sometimes referred to as failover and failback support. The redundancy that HA creates is critical to protect against one or more gateway failures. With HA, the host can continue the I/O with only the possibility of performance latency until the failed gateways are back and functioning correctly.

NVMe-oF gateways are virtually grouped into gateway groups and the HA domain sits within the gateway group. An NVMe-oF gateway group supports eight gateways. Each NVMe-oF gateway in the gateway group can be used as a path to any of the subsystems or namespaces that are defined in that gateway group. HA is effective with two or more gateways in a gateway group.
 
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 An NVMe-oF gateway can only be part of one gateway group and should never be part of two or more gateway groups.

High Availability is enabled by default. To use High Availability, a minimum of two gateways and listeners must be defined. For more information, see Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway.

It is important to create redundancy between the host and the gateways. To create a fully redundant network connectivity, be sure that the host has two Ethernet ports that are connected to the gateways over a network with redundancy (for example, two network switches).

The HA feature uses the Active/Standby approach for each namespace. Using Active/Standby means that at any point in time, only one of the NVMe-oF gateways serve I/O from the host to a specific namespace. To properly use all NVMe-oF gateways, each namespace is assigned to a different load-balancing group. The number of load-balancing groups is equal to the number of NVMe-oF gateways in the gateway group.

With HA, if an NVMe-oF gateway fails, the initiator continues trying to connect. The amount of time that it tries to connect for depends on what is defined for the initiator. For more information about defining the reconnect time for the initiator and general configuration instructions, see Configuring the NVMe-oF gateway initiator.
section_path: Ceph NVMe-oF gateway > High Availability with NVMe-oF gateway group

title: Scaling-out with NVMe-oF gateway
content:
The NVMe-oF gateway supports scale-out. NVMe-oF gateway scale-out supports:
 
- Up to 4 NVMe-oF gateway groups.
- Up to 8 NVMe-oF gateways in a gateway group.
- Up to 128 NVMe-oF subsystems within a gateway group.
- Up to 512 hosts per gateway group.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If more than 512 host are required, contact IBM Support.
- 4096 namespaces per gateway group.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 An NVMe-oF gateway can only be part of one gateway group and should never be part of two or more gateway groups.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The RHEL and ESXi initiators can have smaller NVMe over Fabric namespace discovery limits. Confirm all discovery limits with your software vendor and version.
section_path: Ceph NVMe-oF gateway > Scaling-out with NVMe-oF gateway

title: NVMe Discovery
content:
The IBM Storage Ceph NVMe-oF gateway supports NVMe Discovery. Each gateway instance that runs in the Ceph cluster also runs a Discovery Controller, which reports the IP addresses of all gateways in the group that are configured with listeners.

For configuring information, see Configuring the NVMe-oF gateway initiator.

title: NVMe-oF gateway in-band authentication
content:
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 In-band authentication is supported on an initiator with Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.5 or later. ESX is not supported.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 DH-HMAC-CHAP authentication requires Linux kernel version 6.0.0 or later. Earlier kernel versions, such as Ubuntu 5.15.0-82-generic do not support the required dhchap_secret option.

The Ceph NVMe-oF gateway uses in-band authentication to maintain security against unknown connection requests from unknown initiators. Using the in-band authentication helps ensure appropriate subsystem access only from authorized hosts. NVMe-oF gateway uses SPDK for DH-HMAC-CHAP authentication, allowing users to authenticate with either unidirectional or bidirectional modes.

Table 1 breaks down the two authentication mode types. The difference between unidirectional and bidirectional authentication is if the subsystem has a key. If only the host contains the DH-HMAC-CHAP key, and the subsystem does not, unidirectional authentication is used.

In cases where the subsystem has a key all hosts that are added to the subsystem must also have a key.
 
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Adding a host without a key to a subsystem that contains a key causes failure when running the host add command.

 Key values are stored encrypted. To use DH-HMAC-CHAP authentication keys, you must create an encryption key. For more information about creating an encryption key, see Defining an NVMe-oF subsystem with nvmeof-cli.
 
| Authentication mode type | Description | Direction |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Unidirectional | Target verifies the host | Initiator to target |
| Bidirectional | Target verifies the host Host verifies the target | Initiator to target Target to initiator |

The Ceph NVMe‑oF gateway supports in‑band authentication by using DH‑HMAC‑CHAP to control access between NVMe initiator hosts and NVMe‑oF subsystems. Authentication keys can be configured at different scopes to support deployments that require unique authentication per host connection. For more information, see NVMe‑oF in‑band authentication.

title: NVMe‑oF in‑band authentication
content:
Understand how the NVMe‑oF gateway uses DH‑HMAC‑CHAP in‑band authentication to control access between hosts and NVMe‑oF subsystems.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 DH-HMAC-CHAP authentication requires Linux kernel version 6.0.0 or later. Earlier kernel versions, such as Ubuntu 5.15.0-82-generic do not support the required dhchap_secret option.

The Ceph NVMe‑oF gateway uses in‑band authentication to prevent unauthorized access from unknown initiators. Authentication is performed by using DH‑HMAC‑CHAP and supports both unidirectional and bidirectional authentication models.

In unidirectional authentication, the target verifies the initiator. In bidirectional authentication, both the initiator and the target verify each other by using authentication keys.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Subsystem‑level and controller‑level DH‑HMAC‑CHAP keys are mutually exclusive. If a subsystem has a DHCHAP key defined, controller‑level keys cannot be defined for hosts in that subsystem. If one or more hosts have controller‑level keys defined, defining or changing a subsystem‑level key is not allowed. Operations that violate these constraints fail.
section_path: NVMe‑oF in‑band authentication

title: Authentication key scope
content:
DH‑HMAC‑CHAP authentication keys define how authentication is applied for hosts accessing a subsystem.

Authentication keys can be defined at different scopes, allowing administrators to choose between simplified configuration and per‑host isolation.

Subsystem scope
A key defined on a subsystem applies to all controllers created for hosts that access the subsystem.
Controller (host) scope
A key defined for a specific host applies only to the controller created for that host, enabling unique authentication per host connection.

title: NVMe-oF gateway performance best practices
content:
Use the NVMe-oF gateway performance best practices to ensure that you are using the gateway to its fullest capacity.

For high IOPS requirements, use a dedicated host for the NVMe-oF gateway.
 
1. Colocation with OSDs is possible, but the high CPU demand from the gateway might introduce CPU contention especially for write client workloads and when the node has multiple OSDs.
2. For dedicated gateways, the gateway needs a minimum of 16 cores. For higher performance requirements, use 30 or more cores.

title: Deployment best practices
content:
The NVMe-oF gateway service automatically stores the service configuration in a pool called `.nvmeof`.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Deploying multiple NVMe-oF gateway groups on different Ceph Block Device-enabled pools (RBD application-enabled pools) is supported but not recommended.

Ceph NVMe-oF gateway uses Linux huge pages by default to improve memory performance. To configure the Ceph NVMe-oF gateway to run without huge pages, see Configuring the gateway to run without huge pages.

title: Rule of Thumb (RoT) sizing guide
content:
The following RoT sizing is based on the mixed workload scenario at latencies less than or equal to 10 ms, with an environment based on 100 Gb networking, with 72 namespaces.
 
| IOPS goal | Number of reactor cores | Total CPU demand (cores) | tgt_cmd_extra_rags specification parameter |
| ------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| Up to 100,000 | 1 | 16 | --cpumask=0x1 |
| Up to 200,000 | 2 | 18 | --cpumask=0x3 |
| Up to 250,000 | 4 | 22 | --cpumask=0xF (default) |
| Up to 300,000 | 8 | 30 | --cpumask=0xFF |

title: Modifying the cores
content:
Use this procedure to modify the cores that are used by Storage Performance Development Kit (SPDK) to handle the I/O.

For more information about specification files, see Managing gateways with a specification file.
 
1. Fetch the specification file of the cluster or a service.
 
- Get the set of specification files for the entire cluster.
 
```bash
ceph orch ls --export > FILE.yaml
```
- Get the set of specification files for a specific NVMe-oF service.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Modify the command to specify the specific NVMe-oF service that is needed.

```bash
ceph orch ls nvmeof --export > nvme-spec.yaml
```
2. Modify the file to include or modify the tgt_cmd_extra_args parameter.
 For example, change from the default tgt_cmd_extra_args: --cpumask=0xF to tgt_cmd_extra_args: --cpumask=0xFF.
 
 
```bash
service_type: nvmeof
service_id: nvmeof.GROUP_NAME
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME
spec:
 pool: .nvmeof
 tgt_cmd_extra_args: --cpumask=0xFF
```

`FF` is a hexadecimal bit mask that is based on the number of cores that are used in the cluster.
 In the following example, 8 cores are used, so the value of `--cpumask` is `0xFF`. For 6 cores, the value is `0x3F`.
 
 
```
[ceph: root@host01/ ]# cat file.yaml
service_type: nvmeof
service_id: nvmeof.group1
placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02
spec:
 pool: .nvmeof
 tgt_cmd_extra_args: --cpumask=0xFF
```
3. Redeploy the service.
 
 
```bash
ceph orch apply -i FILE.yaml
```
4. Reconfigure the NVMe-oF gateway.
 
 
```bash
ceph orch reconfig nvmeof.nvmeof.GROUP_NAME
```

 
 For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01/ ]# ceph orch reconfig nvmeof.nvmeof.group1
```
section_path: NVMe-oF gateway performance best practices > Modifying the cores

title: VMware ESX recommendations
content:
1. Allocate more of the smaller datastores instead of a few large datastores. This approach does not carry capacity cost as Ceph has thin provisions by default and helps ensure that Ceph I/O contexts are available for the gateway.
2. Consider isolating applications with high I/O demands to use a dedicated datastore to ensure adequate host adapter queue depth.
3. Use jumbo frames when possible for ESXi to Gateway network links. Using jumbo frames is beneficial for workloads that use larger I/O block sizes.

title: NVMe-oF in a stretch cluster
content:
When NVMe-oF gateways are deployed across multiple sites, stretch cluster support introduces location-aware failover, failback control, and namespace placement to optimize performance and resilience.

Deploying NVMe-oF gateways across multiple sites can lead to inefficient failover selection, uncontrolled failback behavior, and suboptimal namespace placement. Stretch cluster support enhances IBM Storage Ceph capabilities by introducing location-aware behavior for gateways and namespaces, enabling more predictable failover and improved I/O locality.

Location-aware failover selection
NVMe-oF gateways can be assigned a location attribute that represents their physical site or region.
 
Failover and failback algorithms use this attribute to prioritize gateways in the same location, ensuring that NVMe-oF traffic remains local whenever possible and avoiding cross-site failover to remote gateways when a local gateway is available.

Controlled failback behavior
Stretch cluster support introduces a disaster state for each location, allowing administrators to control failover and failback behavior.
 
When a location is marked as in a disaster state, it is excluded from failover decisions and automatic failback is prevented until the state is cleared, avoiding premature failback to a location that is not yet ready for service.

Location-aware namespace placement
Namespaces can be assigned a location attribute to define their preferred site.
 
The enhanced load-balancing algorithm uses this attribute to place namespaces on gateways in the same location whenever possible, improving I/O locality and avoiding unnecessary cross-site traffic for active workloads.

Automatic namespace relocation and validation
Namespace location assignments are validated against configured gateway locations to ensure consistency.
 
Invalid location assignments are rejected, and if a namespace becomes orphaned, it is automatically relocated to a valid gateway, preventing loss of access due to location inconsistencies.
section_path: NVMe-oF in a stretch cluster

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A deployed and operational IBM Storage Ceph stretch cluster spanning two sites.
 
For more information, see Stretch clusters for Ceph storage
- At least four Ceph nodes per site.
- NVMe-oF gateways deployed in both sites.
 
For more information, see Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway.
- NVMe-oF initiator hosts, such as VMware ESXi systems.
- Network connectivity between sites with controlled latency, typically in the range of 2–10 milliseconds.
section_path: Configuring NVMe-oF in a stretch cluster > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
NVMe-oF stretch clustering extends IBM Storage Ceph across a minimum of two sites and requires site-aware deployment of storage, gateways, and initiators.

Use this information for initial NVMe-oF stretch cluster configuration. For NVMe-oF stretch cluster management information, see Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior.
section_path: Configuring NVMe-oF in a stretch cluster > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Set the location of each NVMe-oF gateway.
The NVMe-oF gateway location defines the physical site of each gateway and do not need to match the Ceph CRUSH roles.
 
Run the following command for each gateway:

```bash
ceph nvme-gw set-location GW_ID POOL_NAME GROUP_NAME LOCATION
```

Gateways are assigned to their respective locations.
2. Configure NVMe-oF subsystems and listeners.

For more information, see:

- Defining an NVMe-oF subsystem
- Managing listeners

 NVMe-oF targets are configured and accessible.
3. Create namespaces with a defined location.
Use the --location parameter in the ceph nvmeof namespace add command.
 
This ensures namespaces are placed on gateways in the same location, when possible.

```bash
ceph nvmeof namespace add --nqn NQN --location LOCATION
```

For more information, see Managing namespaces.

For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# ceph nvmeof namespace add --nqn nqn.2016-06.io.spdk:cnode1.group1 --location DC2
Success
```

Namespaces are created with location-aware placement.

title: What to do next
content:
Validate NVMe-oF connectivity and failover behavior across locations.

1. Verify that stretch mode is enabled correctly.

title: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior
content: Managing NVMe-oF stretch cluster behavior by controlling failover, failback, and namespace placement across gateway locations.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A configured NVMe-oF stretch cluster with gateways assigned to locations.
- Existing NVMe-oF subsystems and namespaces assigned to locations.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > Before you begin

title: About this task
content: After configuration, NVMe-oF stretch cluster deployments can be adjusted by controlling gateway location state and namespace placement. These operations affect failover behavior, failback control, and load balancing between sites.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > About this task

title: Managing NVMe-oF site in disaster state
content: Control failover and failback behavior in an NVMe-oF stretch cluster by marking a gateway location as in a `disaster` state.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > Managing NVMe-oF site in disaster state

title: About this task
content:
When a site is in a disaster or degraded state, it is recommended to mark the gateways in that location as in a `disaster` state.
 
Setting the gateways in a `disaster` state allows administrators to control failback timing during recovery. Without setting the `disaster` state, the NVMe-oF control plane automatically fails back traffic to a site as soon as it becomes reachable.

In some scenarios, automatic failback is not desired. For example, failback can be delayed until the underlying storage layers, such as OSDs, are fully verified and stable.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 When a location is set to a `disaster` state, failback to that location does not occur until the disaster state is cleared.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Set the `disaster` state for a location.

```bash
ceph nvme-gw disaster-set POOL_NAME GROUP_NAME LOCATION
```

 The following example prevents failover back to the DC3 location during recovery:
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# ceph nvme-gw disaster-set pool01 group01 DC3
```

The specified location is excluded from failover selection and automatic failback to that location is blocked.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > Procedure

title: Managing failback behavior
content: Restore a location in an NVMe-oF stretch cluster by clearing its `disaster` state and enabling failback.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > Managing failback behavior

title: About this task
content: Clearing the `disaster` state allows the location to participate in failover selection and triggers a failback, if needed.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Clear the `disaster` state for a location.

```bash
ceph nvme-gw disaster-clear POOL_NAME GROUP_NAME LOCATION
```

For example,
 
```bash
[root@host01 ~]# ceph nvme-gw disaster-clear pool01 group01 DC3
```

The location becomes eligible for failover, and workloads can return to that site.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > Procedure

title: Managing namespace placement
content: Change the location of a namespace in an NVMe-oF stretch cluster to control data placement across sites.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > Managing namespace placement

title: About this task
content: Namespace location determines the preferred gateway site for I/O operations and is used by the load-balancing algorithm.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Change the namespace location.

```bash
ceph nvmeof namespace update --nqn NQN --nsid NSID --location LOCATION
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- The specified location must exist on a gateway in the group.
- Invalid location assignments are rejected.

For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# ceph nvmeof namespace update --nqn nqn.2016-06.io.spdk:cnode1.group1 --nsid ns1 --location DC2
```

The namespace is reassigned to a new preferred location.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify that the namespace is served by a gateway in the expected location.

1. List namespace information by using the NVMe‑oF CLI.
2. Identify the gateway servicing the namespace.
3. Confirm that the gateway location matches the namespace location.

For example,
 
```bash
ceph nvmeof namespace list --nqn NQN

ceph nvme-gw listeners POOL_NAME GROUP_NAME
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Namespace placement is optimized based on location. If a matching gateway location is not available, the system assigns the namespace to another available gateway.
section_path: Managing NVMe‑oF stretch cluster behavior > What to do next

title: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway
content: The Ceph NVMe-oF gateway is the NVMe-oF target node and also a Ceph client node. The Ceph NVMe-oF gateway can be a stand-alone node or be collocated on a Ceph Object Storage Daemon (OSD) node.
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway

title: Before you begin
content:
Installing the NVMe-oF gateway requires a storage system that is running IBM Storage Ceph 8.0 or later cluster.
 
Use this information to install the Ceph NVMe-oF gateway with the `cephadm` command-line interface. To deploy and manage the NVMe-oF gateway with the Ceph Dashboard, see Managing the Ceph NVMe-oF gateway.

For multi-gateway group deployment, repeat any deployment method to configure newer NVMe-oF services.
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 When planning to use in-band authentication, install the NVMe-oF service by using the service specification.
 
For more information, see Deploying by using a service specification file.

If deployment is not done through the service specification, the specification file can be modified at any point to include the encryption key.

For more information, see step 2 of Deploying by using a service specification file. Be sure to use the ceph orch apply command to apply the changes.
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Complete the following steps to install the Ceph NVMe-oF gateway.
Deploy NVMe-oF daemons.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:

- High Availability is enabled by default. To use High Availability, a minimum of two gateways and listeners must be defined.
- Ensure an NVMe-oF gateway node is always part of single gateway group.
- Gateway group names must be unique.

Deploy NVMe-oF daemons by using one of the following methods:
 
- Deploying by specifying the number of daemons and hostnames
- Deploying by adding labels to the hosts
- Deploying by using a service specification file
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > Procedure

title: Deploying by specifying the number of daemons and hostnames
content:
Deploy an `nvmeof` daemon by specifying the number of daemons and hostnames, using the ceph orch apply nvmeof command.
 
```bash
ceph orch apply nvmeof NVME-OF_GROUP_NAME --placement="NUMBER_OF_NODES NODE1 NODE2,..."
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply nvmeof nvmeof_group01 --placement="2 host01 host02"
```

Similarly, add the more gateway groups by deploying `nvmeof` services on Ceph nodes that are not part of any other gateway group. The following example is for `nvmeof_group2`.
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply nvmeof nvmeof_group2 --placement="2 host04 host05"
```
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > Deploying by specifying the number of daemons and hostnames

title: What to do next
content:
The ceph orch apply command does not automatically redeploy the service specification changes. Manually redeploy the NVMe-oF service specification changes on the Ceph Orchestrator to complete implementing the changes.
 
```bash
ceph orch redeploy nvmeof.SERVICE_NAME
```

 For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch redeploy nvmeof.nvmeof-pool
Scheduled to redeploy nvmeof.nvmeof-pool.a-rhel9-node2.blhrht on host 'a-rhel9-node2'
```
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > What to do next

title: Deploying by adding labels to the hosts
content: Add labels to the hosts and set up the daemons by using the labels.
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > Deploying by adding labels to the hosts

title: About this task
content:
For more information about adding and removing host labels, see Managing NVMe-oF gateway host labels.
 
When planning to deploy multiple gateway groups, maintain identical labels on gateways that will be part of same gateway group and change the label information in these steps, as needed.
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Add a label to the host.

```bash
ceph orch host label add NODE LABEL
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch host label add host01 nvmeof_label
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch host label add host02 nvmeof_label
```

In this example, the NODE name is host01 and host02 and the LABEL is nvmeof_label.
2. Display the labels associated with the host.

```bash
ceph orch host ls
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch host ls
HOST ADDR LABELS STATUS
host01 mon,mgr,_admin,nvmeof_label
host02 mon,mgr,_admin,nvmeof_label
```
3. Apply the daemons with the labels added in step 1.

```bash
ceph orch apply nvmeof NVME-OF_GROUP_NAME --placement="label:LABEL"
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply nvmeof nvmeof_group01 --placement="label:nvmeof_label"
```
4. Redeploy the NVMe-oF service.

```bash
ceph orch redeploy nvmeof.POOL_NAME.GROUP_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch redeploy nvmeof.nvmeof-pool
Scheduled to redeploy nvmeof.nvmeof-pool.a-rhel9-node2.blhrht on host 'a-rhel9-node2'
```
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > Procedure

title: Deploying by using a service specification file
content: Install NVMe daemons by using the service specification file.
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > Deploying by using a service specification file

title: About this task
content:
For more information about adding and removing hosts with the service specification file, see Managing gateways with a specification file. To obtain optimal performance when first starting the gateway, consider the Ceph NVMe-oF gateway best practices per NVMe-oF gateway performance best practices.

If modifying cores, during initial deployment start from step 2 of Modifying the cores within NVMe-oF gateway performance best practices.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 mTLS can be configured during deployment or at a later stage. To add mTLS during deployment, see Configuring mTLS authentication.
section_path: Deploying the NVMe-oF gateway > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create a specification file.

```bash
service_type: nvmeof
service_id: .nvmeof.NVME-OF_GROUP_NAME
service_name: SERVICE_TYPE.nvmeof.NVME-OF_GROUP_NAME
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME1
 - HOST_NAME2
spec:
 group: NVME-OF_GROUP_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# cat file.yaml
service_type: nvmeof
service_id: .nvmeof.nvmeof_group01
service_name: nvmeof..nvmeof.nvmeof_group01
placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02
spec:
 pool: .nvmeof
 group: nvmeof_group01
```
2. When using in-band authentication, create an encryption key.

1. Create the encryption key.

```bash
openssl req -newkey rsa:512 -noenc -noout -keyout encryption.key -batch 2> /dev/null
```
2. Copy the encryption and place it in specification file.

```bash
service_type: nvmeof
service_id: .nvmeof.NVME-OF_GROUP_NAME
service_name: SERVICE_TYPE..nvmeof.NVME-OF_GROUP_NAME
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME1
 - HOST_NAME2
spec:
 encryption_key: |
 -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
 ENCRYPTION_KEY
 -----END PRIVATE KEY-----
 pool: .nvmeof
 group: nvmeof_group01
```
3. Deploy the NVMe daemons on the admin node.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i NVME_FILE
```
4. Redeploy the NVMe-oF service.

```bash
ceph orch redeploy nvmeof.POOL_NAME.GROUP_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch redeploy nvmeof.nvmeof-pool
Scheduled to redeploy nvmeof.nvmeof-pool.a-rhel9-node2.blhrht on host 'a-rhel9-node2'
```

title: Using ceph nvmeof commands
content:
Use the integrated `ceph nvmeof` command for seamlessly using NVMe-oF gateway commands from within the IBM Storage Ceph command-line interface.

The integrated `ceph nvmeof` command set helps simplify using the NVMe-oF gateway within the IBM Storage Ceph command-line interface (CLI). With the `nvmeof` integration in place, it is no longer required to use Docker or an alias and the server address (traddr) is taken directly from the provided NQN.

Use the ceph nvmeof --help or ceph nvmeof -h command at any time to view all NVMe-oF commands, their parameters, and descriptions.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The following are interchangeable within ceph nvmeof commands:
 
- `gateway` and `gw`
- `namespace` and `ns`

Table 1 provides ceph nvmeof command parameters and their descriptions.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For real‑time monitoring of gateway CPU and subsystem I/O performance, see Monitoring NVMe-oF performance with ceph nvmeof top.

| Parameter | Description |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| --adrfam:int | IPv type. Input type: Integer. Allowed value types are 0 for IPv4 and 1 for IPv6. |
| --block_size<int> | Provide the block size in megabytes. Input type: Integer |
| --dhchap_controller_key | Specifies a DH‑HMAC‑CHAP key that is used only for the controller created for a specific host. Input type: String |
| --create-image | Create an image within any Ceph Block Device (RBD) application-enabled pool. Note: The --rbd_image_size parameter must be used together with --create-image. |
| --dhchap_key | Use this flag to add a generated DH-HMAC-CHAP key for use with bidirectional in-band authentication. Input type: String |
| --format | View the output for each of these commands in any of the following format options: text, json, yaml, plain, or python. If not specified, the default is text. |
| --gw_group | Use the optional --gw_group at any time to specify a specific gateway group in the ceph nvmeof command. The GW_GROUP value is a user defined string. Input type: String |
| --host_nqn | NQN of the host. |
| --nqn | Subsystem NQN Important: NQN value must not contain an underscore character. |
| --nsid | Specify the namespace ID of the subsystem. Note: When this parameter is not used with add or create commands, the gateway automatically generates an NSID value, the next available value on the subsystem, starting with 1. |
| --psk | TLS Pre-Shared Key (PSK). |
| --rbd_image_size | Provide the Ceph Block Device image size. When provided as a string, the set value is used. When provided as an integer the value is read as megabytes (MBs), by default. Supported size units are as follows: KB, KiB, MB, MiB, GB, GiB, TB, and TiB. Input type: String. |
| --serial-number | If the serial number is not specified, the number is randomly generated. Input type: String |
| --server-address | Use the optional --server-address parameter to specify a particular gateway IP address in the nvmeof command. Use this parameter when you need to connect to a specific gateway in the group. If you do not set it, the CLI selects an arbitrary gateway to run the command. The default port value is 5500. |
| --trsvcid | Port number. The default port value is 4420. Note: To define the IP port on the gateway, be sure to include the --trsvcid information. |
| --uuid | Specify the namespace UUID. When multiple namespaces exist on the same subsystem, each namespace has its own UUID. Note: When this parameter is not used, the gateway automatically generates a UUID value. |

Table 2 compares the deprecated and newer command parameters and their descriptions.
section_path: Using ceph nvmeof commands (part 1)

title: Using ceph nvmeof commands
content:
| Deprecated nvmeof-cli parameter | New ceph nvmeof parameter |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| N/A | gw_group |
| gw get_log_level | gateway get_log_level |
| gw info | gateway info |
| gw version | gateway version |
| output | N/A |
| rbd-create-image | create-image |
| rbd-image | rbd_image_name |
| rbd-trash-image-on-delete | trash-image |
| server-port | traddr |
| size | rbd_image_size |
| subsystem | nqn |
| traddr | server-address |

For more information about using `nvmeof-cli` commands, see Using the nvmeof-cli utility for configuring and managing NVMe-oF gateways.
